reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline variants in the RB1 tumour suppressor gene, inherited autosomal dominantly with high penetrance, and is the prototypical example of Knudson's two-hit hypothesis
The commonest childhood intraocular malignancy, typically presenting before school age with leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex) or strabismus
Heritable disease is characteristically bilateral and multifocal and presents at a younger age than sporadic unilateral tumours
A positive family history or bilateral disease strongly indicates a germline RB1 variant, but many heritable cases arise de novo without an affected parent
Germline carriers have a markedly increased risk of second, non-ocular cancers later in life, especially osteosarcoma, soft-tissue sarcoma, and melanoma
This second-cancer risk is amplified within fields exposed to radiotherapy, so external-beam radiation is minimised in favour of other treatment modalities where feasible
Trilateral retinoblastoma, an associated intracranial (typically pineal) tumour, is a recognised and serious complication in germline carriers
Early diagnosis with globe- and vision-sparing treatment and lifelong surveillance for second malignancies are central to management, alongside genetic counselling and testing of relatives
reference.pathophysiology: RB1 encodes the retinoblastoma protein, a key regulator of the cell cycle that restrains progression from G1 to S phase. In heritable disease a germline loss-of-function variant is present in every cell, so a single additional somatic hit inactivating the remaining allele in a developing retinal cell is sufficient to initiate a tumour; this explains the early-onset, bilateral, multifocal pattern. The universal germline defect also predisposes other tissues to malignancy throughout life and heightens sensitivity to the mutagenic effects of ionising radiation.
additionalDifferentials: Coats disease and other causes of leukocoria
Persistent fetal vasculature and retinopathy of prematurity
Toxocariasis and other intraocular inflammatory lesions
additionalInvestigations: Germline RB1 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, including tumour analysis where available, with genetic counselling
Examination under anaesthesia with dilated fundoscopy for diagnosis and monitoring
Ocular ultrasound and MRI to characterise the tumour and assess extraocular or optic nerve spread
Brain MRI surveillance for trilateral (pineal) disease in germline carriers
Long-term surveillance for second primary malignancies in germline carriers
redFlags: Leukocoria or new strabismus in a young child requiring urgent ophthalmic referral
Bilateral disease or a positive family history indicating heritable retinoblastoma
Neurological or pineal-region symptoms suggesting trilateral retinoblastoma
New bony or soft-tissue mass in a survivor, particularly within a previously irradiated field, suggesting a second cancer
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and modern eye-preserving treatment, survival from the intraocular tumour is excellent in well-resourced settings, though outcome worsens markedly with extraocular spread or delayed presentation. For germline carriers, long-term prognosis is shaped by the substantial lifetime risk of second malignancies, making lifelong surveillance essential.
pitfalls: Delaying referral for leukocoria or strabismus and allowing extraocular tumour spread
Assuming an absent family history excludes heritable disease, since de novo germline variants are common
Using external-beam radiotherapy without weighing the heightened radiation-associated second-cancer risk in germline carriers
Discharging survivors from follow-up and missing later second primary cancers
